title: Basil Adoption Notice
tests: Subject-as-artifact sample: a living basil plant's identity rendered as an adoption notice, plant passport, care card, leaf sample, placement map, and botanical keepsake packet.
prompt:
Use case: product-mockup
Asset type: GPT Image 2 subject-as-artifact archive image
Primary request: Create a polished 1024x1536 vertical image titled conceptually "Basil Adoption Notice", where a living basil plant's identity becomes a handled adoption packet and botanical keepsake.

Scene/backdrop: an overhead archival photograph on a small kitchen table in soft morning light. The subject is not just a plant portrait; it is represented through a physical packet of artifacts: an adoption notice, tiny passport booklet, pressed leaf sleeve, pot-placement map, watering stamp card, handwritten care tag, seed envelope, and a small instant photo of the basil in its pot. Include a few real basil leaves and a bit of soil dust around the packet.

Subject identity: make the basil feel like a specific little character without making it cartoonish. Its identity should come through the records: a name line, growth habit notes, favorite window, leaf scent swatch, watering history stamps, pruning marks, and "kitchen placement" diagram. Use sparse large readable labels only: "BASIL ADOPTION NOTICE", "NAME", "SUN", "WATER", "WINDOW", "LEAF SAMPLE", "CARE CARD", "ADOPTED". Other small marks may be believable pseudo-notation.

Composition/framing: vertical 9:16, straight-down with real paper thickness, creases, translucent sleeve glare, pressed leaf texture, stamped ink, paper fibers, folded corners, green pencil marks, twine, and a small brass clip. The adoption notice should be the main artifact, with the passport and care card partly tucked beneath it. Make it immediately read as subject identity becoming a record/keepsake, not a generic plant care poster.

Lighting/mood: warm morning kitchen light, fresh green basil, cream paper, soft terra-cotta accents, botanical ink, gentle shadows, tactile realism, hopeful and slightly funny but not cute-cartoon.

Constraints: no generic infographic poster, no measuring device, no dashboard, no app UI, no real logos, no brand names, no watermark, no signature, no people, no copyrighted characters, no dancing or performance imagery, no dense tiny text. The plant's identity must visibly become the artifact.

subjectArtifact.description: A specific basil plant represented through an adoption notice, plant passport, care card, pressed leaf sample, placement map, and small keepsake photo.

prompt:

The largest object should be the folded newspaper feature, with smaller identity artifacts tucked around it. Make it immediately read as a human life translated into a newspaper/archive object, not a generic poster or magazine cover.

Lighting/mood: warm desk lamp over cool pre-dawn newsroom shadows, gray newsprint, red pencil marks, blue-black ink, worn manila folder, coffee stains, tactile realism, thoughtful and humane but not sentimental.

Constraints: no real person, no celebrity, no real newspaper logo, no brand names, no app UI, no smartphone, no measuring device, no dashboard, no watermark, no signature, no dense tiny text, no dancing or performance imagery. The person's identity must visibly become the artifact.

title: Old Oak Accession Drawer
tests: Subject-as-artifact physical accession-drawer example; tests identity becoming a handled specimen/keepsake object rather than a flat document or normal tree portrait. Exact generated PNG provenance verified.
prompt:
Create a finished cinematic square photograph of Old Oak Accession Drawer, a subject-as-artifact image where a specific 120-year-old red oak called Number 17 has become a handled museum accession object rather than a normal tree portrait or a flat poster. Show a shallow open oak museum drawer pulled out on a conservation table, viewed at a natural three-quarter angle. Inside the drawer, arrange the tree's identity artifacts: a bark rubbing on thin translucent tissue, a small polished cross-section ring sample in a brass cradle, pressed red-oak leaves under glassine corners, acorn caps in a tiny unlabeled porcelain dish, a blue ribbon fragment pinned beside a thread tag, soil grains in a stoppered vial, a sparse hand-drawn block map, a small neighborhood history card, a blank accession tag, and warm brass specimen pins. Include worn drawer runners, green felt, linen tape, graphite smudges, dust, scratches, fingerprints on glassine, tiny splinters, wax seal residue, conservation weights, cotton gloves resting aside with no visible hands, a magnifier, raking late-afternoon window light, warm amber highlights, and cool window fill. Make the artifact form visually dominant and emotionally specific: the viewer should understand one individual old oak has become a record, keepsake, specimen, and neighborhood memory packet. Sparse readable labels are allowed only where natural to accession materials. Avoid a plain sheet of paper, poster, parchment layout, generic tree photo, dashboard, QR code, barcode, real logos, official institution names, people, hands, faces, dancing imagery, watermark, signature, and prompt-instruction text.

Source photo needed: optional reference photo of a human, animal, or plant; otherwise invent a coherent subject.

Reusable fill-in-the-blank template: Create a finished subject-as-artifact image of [SUBJECT] as a tree identity displayed in a museum accession drawer with [BARK OR SURFACE SAMPLE], [LEAF/FUR/PORTRAIT/FEATURE SAMPLE], [HISTORY TOKEN], [LOCATION CLUE], [IDENTITY TAG], and [MEMORY OBJECT]. Make the subject's identity become a handled artifact someone could file, carry, display, trade, stamp, archive, or discover. Preserve the subject's key identity traits when a reference photo is supplied; otherwise invent a specific believable subject. Use tactile materials, storage context, wear, evidence of handling, sparse natural labels, and a physical drawer, tray, box, vitrine, or cabinet system rather than a flat poster.

What to preserve: supplied identity traits, species or subject type, silhouette, markings, growth habit or body cues, distinctive damage, meaningful personal history, source-photo angle when useful, and any emotionally important details.

What to change: transform the live subject or source photo into a handled archive object made from specimen samples, keepsake tokens, accession materials, map fragments, labels, drawer hardware, protective sleeves, conservation tools, and cinematic physical lighting.

Optional negative constraints: no generic portrait/photo with no artifact logic, no fictional measuring dashboard, no plain parchment poster, no dense tiny text, no real logos, no private data, no QR codes, no barcodes, no people or hands unless requested, and keep the source subject recognizable if a photo is supplied.

Example substitution: Use an optional clear photo of a street tree with rough bark and a forked branch; preserve the lightning scar, low branch shape, leaf type, neighborhood context, and any tied ribbons or keepsakes, then turn the tree into an open museum accession drawer with bark rubbing, ring sample, pressed leaves, acorn dish, location map, history card, ribbon fragment, soil vial, specimen pins, and warm conservation-room light.

subjectArtifact.description: A specific old red oak represented through a museum accession drawer with bark rubbing, ring sample, pressed leaves, acorn dish, map fragment, ribbon token, soil vial, and neighborhood history card.
